app.name: Aasra
app.tagline: Step-by-step help for families claiming a deceased person's assets.
app.description: A step-by-step guide for families in India claiming the deceased person's bank accounts, insurance, EPF, shares, and property.
app.legalLine: Aasra is a technology and service platform, not a law firm. The guidance here is not legal advice. A lawyer reviews anything legal before it is filed.
app.notALawFirmShort: A technology and service platform, not a law firm.

nav.findLostMoneyFull: Find lost money on the government portals
nav.recoveryFull: See what the family may be able to recover

home.title: Claim what the deceased person left behind, step by step.
home.lead: Use this app to claim the deceased person's bank accounts, insurance, EPF, shares, and property. The app takes you from the first form to the money reaching your family.
home.planAhead: Plan ahead for your own family
home.reassurance: Free to begin. No will needed. Stop and return at any time.

ask.title: Have a question right now?
ask.body: You do not have to start a claim to ask. Type the question in your own words. The assistant answers in plain language, at any hour.

portals.title: Find accounts the family may not know about
portals.body: Search for forgotten bank accounts, unclaimed shares, provident fund, old insurance policies, and a business registered in the deceased person's name. The app opens the correct official page for each search and explains what to look for.
portals.listLabel: The portals this app takes you to
portals.safety: Run each search yourself, on the official site, in your own browser. This app never asks for a password, a PIN, or a one-time code.

one.title: Step 1: Answer the questions
one.body: Answer one question at a time. You can stop at any point. Your answers are saved automatically.

two.title: Step 2: Add documents
two.body: Upload a photo of any document. The app reads it and sorts the details for you. The app also helps find accounts the family may not know about.

three.title: Step 3: Follow the checklist
three.body: Get a clear list of what each bank or insurer requires. A lawyer reviews anything legal before it is filed.

principle.quote: The app reads documents, prepares drafts, translates text, and sends reminders. Lawyers make all legal decisions.
principle.note: The assistant organises information and explains terms. A qualified lawyer approves anything legal before your family acts on it.

noWill.title: No will
noWill.body: Most families do not have one. The law then decides who inherits. Start the claim in the same way.

unknownAssets.title: Unknown accounts
unknownAssets.body: Old bank accounts, insurance, and EPF are often forgotten. Use the government portals to search for them.

abroad.title: Living abroad
abroad.body: Handle the claim from another country. The app arranges help on the ground in India.

firstTime.title: First time
firstTime.body: No experience with banks or paperwork is needed. Every step is explained in plain words, and a lawyer is available.

business.title: A business
business.body: The deceased person may have run a shop, a firm, or a company. GST, licences, staff, and business accounts are handled too.

closing.title: Start when you are ready
closing.body: Beginning takes a few minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

religion.title: Which faith did the deceased person follow?
religion.body: In India, this answer decides how an estate is divided. A Hindu family and a Christian family divide an estate under different laws. Choose one option to see the law that applies to your family.
religion.note: This answer is required by law, and it stays private. Choose "Prefer not to say" to see the rules that all of India's succession laws share.

intake.label: Questions
intake.title: Step 1: Answer the questions
intake.intro: Answer one question at a time. You can stop at any point and return later. Your answers are saved automatically.

documents.label: Documents
documents.title: Step 2: Add documents
documents.intro: Upload a photo of any document you have: a bank passbook, a policy, an Aadhaar card. If you have no documents yet, continue to the next step.

heirs.label: Heirs
heirs.title: Step 3: Check who inherits
heirs.intro: Based on your answers, this page lists who the law treats as an heir. It also lists the documents each bank or insurer requires.

hiddenAssets.label: Lost money
hiddenAssets.title: Step 4: Search for lost money
hiddenAssets.intro: Search the official government portals for forgotten bank accounts, old insurance policies, provident fund, and unclaimed shares.

case.label: Your case
case.title: Step 5: Track your case
case.intro: See everything you have entered, what has been claimed, and what is still pending. Return to this page at any time.

1.question: Who are you claiming for?
1.help: Enter the name of the deceased person and the relationship to you. Nothing else is needed now.

deceased_name.label: Full name of the deceased person

2.question: When did the death occur?
2.help: If you do not know the exact date, enter an approximate date. You can correct it later.

3.question: Who is in the immediate family?
3.help: These names decide who inherits. You can add more names at any time.

spouse_name.label: Name of the surviving spouse, if any
spouse_name.placeholder: Leave blank if there is none

4.question: Which accounts do you already know about?
4.help: Enter whatever you know. The app searches for the rest afterwards.

known_assets_note.label: Banks, insurers, or employers you know of
known_assets_note.placeholder: For example: SBI savings account, an LIC policy, employed at Tata Motors

5.question: Which faith did the deceased person follow?
5.help: This answer is required by law. It stays private.

religion.label: Faith of the deceased person
religion.note: In India, the applicable inheritance law depends on this answer. A Hindu family and a Christian family divide an estate differently. This answer stays private, and you may choose not to give it.

6.question: Was there a will?
6.help: Most families in India have no will. If there is no will, the law decides who inherits.

has_will.label: Did the deceased person leave a will?
has_will.note: If there is a will, the will decides who inherits, and the app helps prove the will is genuine. If there is no will, the law sets the shares. Choose "Not sure" if you do not know, and you can check together with a lawyer.

7.question: Is the mother of the deceased person living?
7.help: Under Hindu law a surviving mother inherits an equal share. Leaving the mother out would make the shares wrong.

mother_living.label: Is the mother of the deceased person living?

mother_name.label: Name of the mother, if known

8.question: Two final questions
8.help: These two answers show whether extra paperwork is required, so that nothing comes as a surprise later.

assets_abroad.label: Did the deceased person own anything outside India?
assets_abroad.note: This includes a bank account, property, or a policy in another country. This adds steps to the claim, and all of them are manageable.

owned_business.label: Did the deceased person run a business, or work for self?
owned_business.note: This includes a shop, a firm, a company, or freelance work. A business is handled differently from a salary.

9.question: Four optional questions
9.help: Every question on this page can be skipped. Each answer makes the recovery estimate more exact, and the estimate still works without any of them.

employed_at_death.label: Was the deceased person employed at the time of death?
employed_at_death.note: If the answer is yes, provident fund, death insurance under EDLI, and gratuity may all be due to the family. Many families are never told about the death insurance.

years_of_service.label: Roughly how many years did the deceased person work?
years_of_service.note: An approximate number is useful. Used together with the salary below to estimate the provident fund and the gratuity.

last_monthly_salary.label: Approximate last monthly salary, in rupees
last_monthly_salary.note: Enter the monthly figure, not the annual one. A payslip or a bank statement will show it.

property_state.label: In which state is any property or land likely to be?
property_state.note: This picks the correct state land record portal. Leave it blank if there is no property, or if the state is not known.

insurance.note: The policy number is the useful part.

will.note: Most families do not have one. That is normal.

heirs.nothingBody: Enter the name of a surviving spouse, the children, or whether the mother of the deceased person is living. This page then lists who the law treats as an heir, and what each bank or insurer requires.
heirs.demoNotice: This is a sample result, shown with a fictional family.
heirs.demoTitle: Who the law treats as an heir
heirs.demoBody: No will was found, so the estate is shared between the closest family in equal parts.
heirs.demoWhy: Reason: with no will, the Hindu Succession Act gives the spouse, each child, and the mother an equal share.

summary.will: Because there is a will, the will decides who inherits, not the general law. The next job is different: the app helps you show the will is genuine, and helps get the will accepted by the banks and offices that ask for it.
summary.nothing: Enter the name of a surviving spouse, the children, or whether the mother of the deceased person is living. This page then shows who the law treats as an heir.
summary.muslim: These are the people most likely to be heirs. No share is shown next to each name, and that is deliberate. Under Muslim personal law the exact fractions depend on which relatives survive and which school of law the family follows. A wrong fraction would be worse than an open question.
summary.privateFaith: You chose not to give the faith of the deceased person, which is your right. These are the closest family, who are heirs under every one of India's succession laws. The exact shares depend on which law applies, so the shares are left open.
summary.unknownFaith: These are the closest family. Once the applicable law is known, this page shows each share.
summary.hinduShares: With no will, the estate is divided equally between the closest family. {count, plural, =1 {Here that is one heir, who takes the whole estate.} other {Here that is # heirs, so each heir takes {top}/{bottom} of the estate.}}
summary.indianSpouseAndChildren: With no will, the surviving spouse takes 1/3 of the estate. The children share the remaining 2/3 of the estate in equal parts.
summary.indianSpouseOnly: With no will and no children, the whole estate goes to the surviving spouse.
summary.indianSpouseAndOthers: With no will and no children, the surviving spouse inherits. You have also entered another close relative, and where there is no child the order between those relatives depends on exactly who survives. The shares are left for a lawyer to set.
summary.indianOnlyChild: With no will and no surviving spouse, the only child inherits the whole estate.
summary.indianChildren: With no will and no surviving spouse, the estate is shared equally between the children.
summary.indianOther: With no spouse and no children, the estate passes to the next closest relatives. The Act sets an order for this that depends on exactly who survives, so the shares are left for a lawyer to set.

caution.will: A will still has to be proved before it is acted on, and parts of a will can be challenged. Bring the will to us and a lawyer will read it with you.
caution.muslim: A lawyer who practises in this area works out each exact share. Do not divide anything within the family on the strength of this page alone.
caution.confirmLaw: A lawyer confirms which law applies and what each share is.
caution.unknownWill: You were not sure whether a will exists. If a will is found, it replaces everything on this page, so search for one before anything is filed.

law.lead: Which law applies, who the law treats as an heir, and the papers each bank or office requires. Nothing here is settled until a lawyer has read it.
law.becausePrivate: You chose not to give the faith of the deceased person
law.becauseUnknown: The faith of the deceased person is not known yet
law.becauseGeneric: Based on the faith you entered

law.nextTitle: To have the shares worked out
law.nextBody: Enter a few details about the family: a surviving spouse, the children, and whether the mother of the deceased person is living. This page then fills in with real names and real shares.

acts.muslim: Muslim personal law (the Shariat Application Act, 1937)

notes.notKnown: Enter the faith of the deceased person. This page then names the law that applies to your family, and explains how an estate is divided under it.
notes.hindu: This Act covers Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, and Jains. That is the Act's own definition, not a statement about these being one faith. Where there is no will, the closest family each take one equal share: a surviving spouse, every child, and a surviving mother alike. Sons and daughters inherit the same.
notes.indian: Where there is no will, a surviving spouse takes 1/3 of the estate, and the children share the remaining 2/3 of the estate in equal parts. With no children, the spouse inherits everything. With no spouse, the children share the estate equally.
notes.muslim: Shares are set by personal law rather than by a single Act of Parliament. The shares depend on exactly which relatives survive and which school of law the family follows. This app names the likely heirs, and a lawyer who practises in this area works out each share. A wrong fraction would be worse than an open question.
notes.private: You would rather not say, which is your right. This app can still show the closest family, who are heirs under every one of India's succession laws. Which law sets the exact shares depends on that answer, so the shares are left for a lawyer.
notes.other: The app confirms which of India's succession laws applies to your family before anything is filed.

hiddenAssets.footnote: Run these searches in any order, or skip them and return later. Anything you find is added to your case, so you do not have to remember it twice.
hiddenAssets.howBody: Each search below is on a government or regulator site. Run each search yourself, in your own browser. The app opens the correct page and explains what to look for.
hiddenAssets.safety: This app never asks you for a password, a PIN, or a one-time code. No honest service needs those to search for money that belongs to your family. If any service asks for them, stop and walk away.
hiddenAssets.howFound: Found something? Type it into the box under that search. It is then added to your case.
hiddenAssets.foundLabel: Did you find anything? Enter it here.
hiddenAssets.foundHelp: Whatever you can see is enough: a bank name, an amount, or a reference number.
hiddenAssets.addedDevice: Added, and saved on this device for now.
hiddenAssets.addedDemo: Added. In demo mode nothing is saved.
hiddenAssets.alsoBody: Two more places where families often find something. There are no buttons here, because an address we have not confirmed is how people end up on a convincing fake site.

udgam.name: Forgotten bank accounts
udgam.what: A single search across India's banks, run by the Reserve Bank. When an account sits untouched for ten years, the money is moved to the RBI and listed here.
udgam.why: Most families never learn about an old account in another city, or one opened decades ago before a move. This is the one place that searches every bank at once.
udgam.placeholder: For example: an SBI account in Nashik, ₹42,000, reference UDG123456

iepf.name: Shares and unpaid dividends
iepf.what: The government's Investor Education and Protection Fund. After seven years unclaimed, company shares and their dividends are transferred here, and they can be claimed back.
iepf.why: Shares bought on paper in the 1980s or 1990s are easy for a family to miss. Such shares do not expire, and are often worth far more now than when they were bought.
iepf.placeholder: For example: 200 shares in Tata Steel, folio A0012345

epfo.name: Provident fund
epfo.what: The Employees' Provident Fund Organisation holds retirement savings from every job the deceased person held, along with a pension and a linked insurance payout.
epfo.why: Money is often left behind at an employer from years ago. The family of someone who was still working may also be owed a pension and an insurance amount that nobody mentioned.
epfo.placeholder: For example: UAN 100123456789, from the years at Tata Motors

irdai.name: Life insurance policies
irdai.what: The insurance regulator. This site explains how to trace a policy and lists every licensed insurer, with the complaint route if an insurer does not answer you.
irdai.why: Families often know a policy existed but cannot find the paperwork. A policy that lapsed, or matured and was never collected, still belongs to the family.
irdai.placeholder: For example: an LIC policy, number 4471xxxx, taken around 2005

mca.name: Companies the deceased person was part of
mca.what: The government's register of every company in India. The free "View Company / LLP Master Data" and "View Signatory Details" searches show which companies a person was a director or a signatory of.
mca.why: A shareholding in a small private company is the asset families miss most often, because no statement arrives in the post to remind anyone it exists. A company set up decades ago is still on this register.
mca.placeholder: For example: a director of a private company registered in Pune, CIN on the certificate

udyam.name: A business in the deceased person's name
udyam.what: The official registration portal for small and medium businesses. "Print / Verify Udyam Registration Certificate" confirms a registration and shows what was registered.
udyam.why: A registered business can hold a bank account, a GST number, a lease, and unpaid invoices. A business also carries obligations as well as value, so knowing it exists stops the family being surprised a year later.
udyam.placeholder: For example: a Udyam registration for a tailoring shop, number on the certificate

mutualFunds.name: Mutual funds
mutualFunds.why: Old folios held under a previous address or an earlier phone number.

postOffice.name: Post office savings
postOffice.why: Small savings schemes and recurring deposits, often opened decades ago.

demoBios.demo-1: Works almost entirely with families after a death: succession certificates, bank transmission, and the paperwork a municipal office requires. Happy to speak to elderly parents directly.
demoBios.demo-2: Calculates shares under Muslim personal law, including where the family follows a particular school, and explains the result to everyone involved before anything is divided.
demoBios.demo-3: Handles probate and letters of administration under the Indian Succession Act, and the extra steps a family living outside India runs into. Takes calls across time zones.
demoBios.demo-4: Handles ancestral land, jointly held flats, and cases where one relative will not sign. Will say plainly when a dispute is not worth fighting.
demoBios.demo-5: A good first conversation if you do not yet know what kind of help you need. Covers nominee claims, EPF, and insurance, and will say honestly when no lawyer is needed at all.

canned.succession: A succession certificate is a document from a civil court stating who may collect a person's money and investments. Banks often require one when there was no will and no nominee. It usually takes a few months. A lawyer prepares the application, and the app can arrange that for you.
canned.probate: Probate is a court confirming that a will is genuine, so that banks and offices will act on it. Probate is only needed where there is a will. A lawyer handles the filing, and the app explains what it involves.
canned.legalHeir: A legal heir certificate is a local government document naming the close family of a deceased person. It is quicker and cheaper than a succession certificate, though some banks will not accept it on its own. The tehsil or municipal office issues it.
canned.bank: For a bank claim you usually need the death certificate, your own ID, the bank's claim form, and the passbook or account number. If you are named as nominee the claim is fairly quick. If not, the bank may require a succession certificate. The app tells you which applies once the account is known.
canned.insurance: For a life insurance claim the insurer normally requires the original policy, the death certificate, the insurer's claim form, and proof of the bank account the money should go to. If the policy document is lost, the insurer can trace it from the policy number or from the deceased person's details.
canned.providentFund: Provident fund money is claimed from EPFO using forms 20, 5-IF, and 10-D, along with the death certificate and Aadhaar. There is often a pension and an insurance amount owed too, which families are rarely told about.
canned.start: Start with the death certificate. Almost every office requires it, and nothing else moves without it. After that, answer whatever questions you can in this app, and the app works out who needs to be told and in what order.
canned.howLong: It varies. A bank claim with a nominee can take a few weeks. A claim needing a court certificate usually takes three to six months. Insurance is often six to eight weeks. The app tells you what is waiting on whom, so that silence never feels like nothing is happening.
canned.shares: Shares cannot be worked out here. The answer depends on which law applies to your family and whether there was a will, and a wrong answer would be serious. Answer the questions in this app and the app sets it out for you, with a lawyer confirming it before anything is filed.
canned.will: If there is a will, the will decides who inherits rather than the general law. The will has to be shown to be genuine first, which is what probate does. Bring the will to us and a lawyer will read it with you and explain it plainly.
canned.documents: The death certificate is the document everything depends on. Beyond that you usually need the deceased person's ID, your own ID, and whatever paperwork relates to the account or policy: a passbook, a statement, or a policy number. Even a photo of an old document helps.
canned.fallback: That cannot be answered just now. You can ask what a document means, what a bank or insurer requires, or what the next step is. To talk to a lawyer instead, use the link at the bottom of this panel.

bank.needs: Death certificate, your ID, the bank's claim form, and a nominee letter or succession certificate.

insurer.needs: Original policy, death certificate, claim form, and proof of your bank account.

epfo.needs: Forms 20, 5-IF, and 10-D, death certificate, and Aadhaar.

shares.needs: A transmission request, death certificate, and a notarised affidavit.

recovery.title: What the family may be able to recover
recovery.lead: An estimated range, built from the statutory formulas and from the figures entered so far. Every number on this page can be opened up to show exactly how it was reached.
recovery.homeBody: Answer a few questions and this app estimates what the family may be able to recover, with the calculation and the official source shown for every figure.
recovery.homeHonesty: An estimate from what you enter. This app cannot look up a real balance, and no app can.
recovery.demoNotice: This is a sample family, so the figures below are worked out from sample answers.
recovery.headlineLabel: Estimated amount the family may be able to recover
recovery.headlineHonesty: This is an estimate based on what you have entered, not a confirmed balance. No app can look up a real bank balance, policy, or land record. Open the calculation below to see every figure and its source.
recovery.nothingCountedTitle: Not enough entered yet to estimate an amount
recovery.nothingCountedBody: Answer the questions about employment, salary, and the accounts already known about, and this page fills in with a range. The places worth searching are listed below in the meantime.
recovery.countedTitle: What is counted in the range
recovery.flaggedTitle: Worth checking, with no amount counted
recovery.flaggedBody: No rupee figure is counted for these, because no honest figure can be produced without searching. Each one is a real place where money is often found, and the portal to search is linked below.
recovery.workingsTitle: Every figure, and where it comes from
recovery.workingsIntro: Each line below shows its range, the arithmetic in plain words, how firm it is, and the official source. Nothing on this page is a guess that cannot be traced back.
recovery.workingsFootnote: The same answers always produce the same figures. Nothing here is randomised, and no figure is a particular person's confirmed balance.
recovery.contextTitle: Why searching is worth the effort
recovery.contextBody: ₹{crore} crore of unclaimed bank deposits is held in the Reserve Bank of India's Depositor Education and Awareness Fund. A balance reaches that fund after {years} years untouched, and it remains claimable from the bank that held it. Most families never learn about an account opened decades ago in another city.
recovery.pursueBody: Each search below is on a government or regulator site. Run each one yourself, in your own browser. This app never asks for a password, a PIN, or a one-time code.
recovery.askAbout: Ask a question about this estimate

basis.reportedDeposits: Read from the amounts you entered: {amounts}. Counted at face value and not adjusted, because these are figures you provided rather than figures this app worked out.
basis.edliRange: Every EPF member in employment at death is covered by the EDLI scheme, at no cost to the employee. The payout is held between the statutory floor of {min} and the statutory ceiling of {max}. The exact figure depends on the average provident fund balance of the last twelve months, which only EPFO can confirm.
basis.edliFromSalary: The EDLI payout is {multiple} times average monthly wages, with wages counted up to the ceiling of {ceiling}, plus a balance-linked part capped at {bonusCap}. Using the salary entered, wages count as {cappedWages}. The result is then held between the statutory floor of {min} and the ceiling of {max}.
basis.epfFromSalaryAndYears: Estimated from the salary of {salary} a month across {years} years of service. The lower figure is the legal minimum: {employeeRate}% of the statutory wage ceiling of {ceiling} each month, which is all an employer is required to contribute on. The higher figure assumes contributions on the full salary from both the employee and the employer, {totalRate}% in all, which many employers in the organised sector do. The range is wide because only EPFO can say which applied. No interest is added, so the real balance is likely to be higher than either figure.
basis.epfDefaultRange: Employment is known, but no salary or length of service was entered, so this is a wide placeholder rather than a calculation. Enter an approximate salary and number of years and this line becomes a real estimate.
basis.gratuityFormula: The statutory formula is {days} divided by {divisor}, multiplied by the last monthly wages, multiplied by the completed years of service. Here that is {days}/{divisor} of {salary} across {years} years, which comes to about {point}. A band of {band}% either side is shown because gratuity is calculated on basic wages and dearness allowance rather than on the full salary. The statutory maximum is {max}.
basis.unclaimedDepositsFlag: A bank balance untouched for {years} years is moved to the Reserve Bank of India's Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, which holds ₹{crore} crore nationally. Whether the deceased person has anything there can only be found by searching the RBI UDGAM portal. No amount is counted here, because no amount can honestly be assumed.
basis.sharesFlag: A dividend left unclaimed for {years} years, and the shares it relates to, are transferred to the IEPF and can be claimed back. Paper share certificates from the 1980s and 1990s are the holdings families miss most often, because nothing arrives in the post as a reminder. No amount is counted, because only a search can show whether anything is held.
basis.lifeInsuranceFlag: A policy number is not a sum assured, so no amount is counted here. If a figure was entered it has already been counted once under the amounts you entered. If the paperwork cannot be found, the IRDAI site explains how to trace a policy and lists every licensed insurer.
basis.propertyFlag: No rupee value is estimated for property or land, deliberately. The value of a plot depends on its exact location, its access, its title, and whether it is agricultural, and no honest figure can be produced from a state name alone. The state land record portal is linked below instead.

assumptions.estimateNotBalance: Every figure here is an estimate or a statutory entitlement, never a confirmed balance. This app does not and cannot read a real bank account, policy, or land record.
assumptions.reportedAtFaceValue: Amounts you entered are counted exactly as entered, with nothing added for interest or growth.
assumptions.edliRequiresMembership: The death insurance figure assumes the deceased person was an EPF member in employment at the time of death. EPFO confirms membership.
assumptions.epfNoInterest: The provident fund estimate counts contributions only and adds no interest, so the real balance is likely to be higher than the range shown.
assumptions.epfDefaultIsPlaceholder: The provident fund range is a placeholder until an approximate salary or length of service is entered.
assumptions.gratuityDeathWaiver: Gratuity normally requires five years of continuous service, but that requirement does not apply where the employment ended in the death of the employee. Gratuity is therefore included however short the service was.
assumptions.gratuityOnBasicWages: Gratuity is calculated on basic wages and dearness allowance rather than on the full salary including allowances, which is why a band is shown rather than a single figure.
assumptions.insuranceNotDoubleCounted: An insurance amount you entered is counted once, under the amounts you entered, and is not counted a second time under life insurance.
assumptions.propertyNotValued: Property and land are not given a rupee value, because no defensible figure can be produced without a valuation.
assumptions.epfCeilingBrackets: The provident fund range is wide on purpose. Contributions are compulsory only on wages up to the statutory ceiling, and contributing on the full salary is common but not required, so the two ends of the range cover both practices. The provident fund passbook on the EPFO portal shows which one applied.

notes.gratuityNeedsSalary: Gratuity is not estimated yet. Enter an approximate last monthly salary and number of years worked, and the statutory formula is applied.
notes.nothingCountedYet: No amount could be counted from the answers entered so far. The categories listed are still worth searching.

landRecords.title: Property and land
landRecords.body: No rupee value is estimated for property or land, because no honest figure can be produced without a valuation. What this app does instead is point you at the correct state land record portal, explain what to search by, and record whatever you find.
landRecords.safety: This app never asks for Aadhaar, PAN, a password, or a one-time code. Search on the official state site yourself, in your own browser, and enter what you find below. Any service that offers to search on your behalf in exchange for those details is a scam.
landRecords.stateLabel: Which state is the property or land in?
landRecords.stateHelp: Pick a state to see its official land record portal.
landRecords.guessedFromPlace: Shown from the town entered earlier. Change the state above if the property is elsewhere.
landRecords.openPortal: Open the official land record portal
landRecords.noPortalBody: The official address for this state has not been confirmed, and this app does not print an address it has not checked. A wrong land record address is how families end up on a convincing fake site. Start from the central land records programme below, which links to each state, or ask a lawyer.
landRecords.openCentral: Open the central land records programme
landRecords.foundLabel: Did you find any property or land? Enter it here.
landRecords.foundHelp: Whatever you can see is enough: a survey number, a village name, or an area.
landRecords.foundPlaceholder: For example: survey number 142/2 at Wagholi village, about 0.4 hectare
landRecords.addedDevice: Added, and saved on this device for now.
landRecords.addedDemo: Added. In demo mode nothing is saved.
landRecords.allStatesTitle: Every state portal this app has confirmed
landRecords.notYetConfirmed: States with no confirmed address yet. These are listed by name rather than linked, because an unverified land record link is not worth the risk.

portals.maharashtra: Search the 7/12 extract, the 8A extract, or a property card. Choose the district, taluka, and village, then enter the survey or gat number.
portals.gujarat: Choose rural land records for a village or urban land records for a city, then search the record of rights.
portals.karnataka: Search the RTC, also called the pahani, by survey number or by the name of the owner. Khata extracts and mutation status are on the same portal.
portals.uttarPradesh: Search the khatauni by district, tehsil, and village, then by khasra number or by the name of the owner.
portals.rajasthan: Search the jamabandi copy for agricultural land by district, tehsil, and village. The online copy is for reference, and a certified copy is applied for at a kiosk.
portals.tamilNadu: Choose the district, taluk, and village, then search the patta or chitta by patta number or by survey number. A subdivision goes in its own field.
portals.telangana: Search the details of land, the encumbrance certificate, and registered document details. Succession applications are made on the same portal.

payment.note: The fee is set by the lawyer and is shown before anything is charged. Payment is handled by Razorpay, and this app never sees or stores a card number.
payment.paidSimulated: Test payment recorded. No real money was charged.
payment.paidNotStored: The payment is confirmed. The record in your case is still catching up, and will appear shortly.
payment.testBody: No payment gateway is set up in this copy of the app, so nothing can be charged. Use the button below to record the fee as paid and see the rest of the flow.
payment.testBodyDegraded: The payment gateway could not be reached just now, so nothing can be charged. Use the button below to record the fee as paid and continue. Nothing real is charged.
payment.cancelled: The payment window was closed, so nothing was charged. You can try again whenever you are ready.
payment.verifyFailed: The payment could not be confirmed, so nothing has been marked paid. If money has left your account it will be returned automatically. Try again, or talk to a lawyer about it.
payment.setupFailed: The payment could not be started just now. Try again in a moment.

consultations.title: Lawyers you have asked for
consultations.emptyBody: No consultation has been requested yet. That is normal, and there is no hurry. When you want a lawyer to look at the case, pick one from the panel and ask.
consultations.demoNotice: A sample request, shown with a fictional lawyer.
consultations.note: A lawyer contacts you directly once the fee is paid. Nothing legal is filed before a lawyer has read the case.
